fieldFixes.summary: On 5 June 2013 The Guardian published a top-secret Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court order, granted on 25 April, requiring Verizon to hand the NSA call records 'on an ongoing, daily basis', including domestic calls. On 6 June The Guardian and The Washington Post both reported an NSA programme called PRISM. The Guardian's story drew on a 41-slide training presentation which said the programme let officials collect search history, email content, file transfers and live chats from Google, Facebook, Apple and other US internet companies. Every company that answered the Guardian denied knowledge of it. The US Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board later dated the first story to 5 June 2013 and described it as the first of a series based on documents disclosed by Edward Snowden.

issues: The summary narrows the Court's exception to 'unless the person's role in public life justifies access'. Paragraph 97 says the rule does not apply 'if it appeared, for particular reasons, such as the role played by the data subject in public life', that the interference is justified by the public's preponderant interest. Public role is one example, not the only ground.

Everything else checks out. Paragraph 97 is the right paragraph number. Operative point 3 confirms delisting 'even, as the case may be, when its publication in itself on those pages is lawful'. The press release confirms the 2010 AEPD complaint and the La Vanguardia pages of January and March 1998 announcing a real-estate auction for social security debts.

fieldFixes.summary: In Case C-131/12, brought after Mario Costeja González complained in 2010 to Spain's data protection agency about search results linking to 1998 La Vanguardia pages announcing a real-estate auction, the Grand Chamber held that a search engine operator processes personal data and can be obliged to remove links to lawful third-party pages from results for a person's name. It held that the data subject's rights under Articles 7 and 8 of the Charter override, as a rule, both the operator's economic interest and the public's interest in finding the information, unless there are particular reasons, such as the person's role in public life, why the public's interest in access prevails.

fieldFixes.summary: Maximillian Schrems, an Austrian Facebook user since 2008, complained to the Irish Data Protection Commissioner that, in light of Snowden's 2013 revelations, US law and practice did not offer sufficient protection against surveillance by public authorities of data transferred there. In Case C-362/14 the Grand Chamber declared the Commission's 2000 Safe Harbour decision (2000/520) invalid, holding that laws allowing public authorities generalised access to the content of electronic communications compromise the essence of the right to private life.
fieldFixes.significance: One individual's complaint knocked out Safe Harbour, the main framework for transatlantic data flows, proving that a person could force the system to answer for where their data goes.

issues: The significance claims that Article 21(5) is 'the first clause in a major privacy law' to anticipate a person's software stating their objection. That 'first' cannot be supported. Recital 66 of Directive 2009/136/EC (the 2009 ePrivacy amendment) already contemplated consent 'expressed by using the appropriate settings of a browser or other application'. California's 2013 amendment to CalOPPA (AB 370) required websites to disclose how they respond to browser 'Do Not Track' signals. Neither is a right to object by automated means, so Article 21(5) may still be the first binding right of its kind, but the unqualified 'first clause' is overstated. EUR-Lex blocked scripted access, so these precedents could not be quote-checked; they are cited only to justify softening the claim.

All factual claims check out: signed 'Done at Brussels, 27 April 2016', OJ L 119 of 4.5.2016, Article 99(2) 'It shall apply from 25 May 2018.', and the texts of Article 21(5) and Article 25(2), with article numbers confirmed in the extracted text. Brussels as the signing place fits the Parliament's Brussels mini-plenary of 27–28 April 2016.

fieldFixes.significance: Article 21(5) was among the first provisions in a major privacy law to give a person a right that their software can exercise for them, objecting 'by automated means using technical specifications'. It is the legal hook on which machine-readable signals such as Global Privacy Control and person-proffered terms can hang.

issues: The significance overstates the holding. It says the judgment extended constitutional privacy 'explicitly to threats from private, non-state actors'. The Court's order declares a right under Article 21 and Part III. Chandrachud J's opinion recognises that dangers 'can originate not only from the state but from non-state actors as well' and commends a data protection law to the Government. Kaul J writes: 'The right to privacy is claimed qua the State and non-State actors. Recognition and enforcement of claims qua non-state actors may require legislative intervention by the State.' So the judgment recognised non-state threats but did not make the constitutional right directly enforceable against them.

Checks passed: the Order of the Court overrules M P Sharma outright and Kharak Singh 'to the extent that it holds that the right to privacy is not protected by the Constitution'. It is signed by all nine judges and dated 'New Delhi; AUGUST 24, 2017'. The order confirms the Chandrachud judgment was delivered for Khehar CJI, Agrawal and Nazeer JJ and himself. Wikipedia independently confirms the 24 August 2017 date and the nine-judge bench.

fieldFixes.significance: Extended constitutional privacy to the world's most populous democracy. Its opinions explicitly recognised that threats to informational privacy come from private, non-state actors holding data as well as from the state, though they noted that enforcing privacy claims against such actors may require legislation.
